meta.blurb: A coded warning, a body in a moated Sussex house, and a face that is not whose it seems. Holmes unravels a murder at Birlstone, then follows it back to a dark valley in Pennsylvania where a secret society ruled by fear.
meta.bible: Sherlock Holmes: the great detective of Baker Street, calm and sharp. Dr Watson: his friend, loyal and honest. Professor Moriarty: the Napoleon of crime, a hidden master of London's underworld. Fred Porlock: his nervous agent, who secretly warns Holmes. Whitaker's Almanack: the yearly reference book that unlocks Porlock's cipher. Part One, The Tragedy of Birlstone: Inspector MacDonald of Scotland Yard, a young Scottish detective. White Mason: the local Sussex inspector. John Douglas: the master of Birlstone Manor, a rich country gentleman who lived long in America and California. Ettie Douglas: his wife. Cecil Barker: his close friend. Ames: the butler. Dr Wood: the local doctor. Birlstone Manor: an old grey house in Sussex, with a moat and a drawbridge raised each night. The dead man: Ted Baldwin, a Scowrer who hunted Douglas for years. The card: V V 341. The mark: a triangle in a circle, burned into the arm. The dumb-bells: a pair, one missing. Part Two, The Scowrers: Vermissa Valley, Pennsylvania, 1875, a coal and iron valley ruled by fear. Jack McMurdo: a bold newcomer, really Birdy Edwards, a detective of Pinkerton's agency; later John Douglas. Jacob Shafter: a kind German storekeeper. Ettie Shafter: his daughter, later Ettie Douglas. Boss McGinty: the Bodymaster of Lodge 341, saloon keeper of the Union House. The Order of Freemen: the public name of the secret society; the Scowrers: its killers. Ted Baldwin: a young Scowrer, Ettie's rival suitor and McMurdo's enemy. Morris: a gentle lodge member who fears the violence. James Stanger: the newspaper editor beaten by the gang. Captain Marvin: of the Coal and Iron Police. Chicago, California, South Africa. The ship Palmyra. Voice and tone: classic Sherlock Holmes, clear and clever; the crimes are stated plainly and without gore; the second half is a darker, quicker adventure. Beat 50 closes the whole book.

B1B2: One morning at Baker Street, Sherlock Holmes receives a letter made almost entirely of numbers. It comes from Porlock, a secret helper who sends warnings to Holmes while working for a very dangerous man.
Holmes explains to Watson that every number must point to a page and a word in a certain book. After some thought he guesses that it is Whitaker's Almanack, which any careful man might own.
The decoded message warns that danger is near for a rich country gentleman called Douglas, who lives at Birlstone House. It ends in a hurry, as if the writer had been interrupted or frightened.
Holmes tells Watson that Porlock works for Professor Moriarty, the greatest criminal mind in England. Moriarty sits at the centre of a huge web, and he rarely does any wrong with his own hands.
Before the morning is over, Inspector MacDonald of Scotland Yard arrives with serious news. John Douglas of Birlstone Manor was murdered in his own house last night.
The three men take the train to Sussex, and MacDonald describes the house on the way. Birlstone Manor is very old and stands behind a moat, with a drawbridge that is pulled up every night.
At the small station they are met by White Mason, the local police inspector, who has been working since dawn. He is a calm, careful man, and he leads them straight to the manor.
At midnight the household heard a loud shot, and Mr Barker and the butler ran to the study. There they found Douglas lying dead on the floor, with a terrible wound from a gun.
Near the body lies a card marked with the letters V V and the number 341. On the dead man's arm there is an old mark, a triangle inside a circle, burned into the skin.
A shotgun with its barrels sawn short lies on the floor beside the body. The window is open, and there is a mark of blood on the sill, as if a man had climbed out.
Cecil Barker tells Holmes that Douglas had lived in America and was always afraid of old enemies. He says the killer must have come in by the window and escaped the same way, across the moat.

Mrs Douglas, the dead man's wife, is quiet and strangely calm, only a few hours after his death. Holmes also notices that Barker, though he talks a great deal, does not seem nearly as shocked as he should.
Holmes walks round the moat and studies the bank below the window with great care. There is no mud, no scratch and no broken grass to show that a man has crossed.
Holmes picks up a heavy dumb-bell from the corner of the study and asks where its partner is. Nobody knows, and he decides that the missing weight is the oddest fact of the whole case.
That night Holmes asks to be left alone in the study, where he smokes and thinks for many hours. By morning he is sure that the tidy story told to the police cannot be the true one.
At Holmes's request, the police search the bottom of the moat beneath the study window. A bundle of clothes is pulled out of the water, tied round the missing dumb-bell.
Holmes tells the two inspectors that the clothes in the bundle belonged to the killer, not to the dead man. The face could not be known, so the dead man had been dressed to look like Douglas.
Holmes goes to Mrs Douglas and Barker and says gently that he knows the truth. The dead man is not John Douglas, and John Douglas, he is sure, is still hiding in the house.
A secret door opens, and a strong, sunburned man steps out into the room. It is John Douglas himself, alive and well, and his wife runs to him.
Douglas tells them that a man named Ted Baldwin crept into the study with the shotgun. In the fight that followed the gun went off, and Baldwin was killed instead of Douglas.
Afraid that Baldwin's friends would come after him, Douglas asked Barker and Ettie for help. Together they dressed the dead man in Douglas's gown, left the card on him and hid Douglas in the house.
Holmes asks why Baldwin hunted Douglas for so many years. Douglas answers that the story began long ago in a dark valley in Pennsylvania, and he starts to tell it.
In the winter of 1875 a young man called Jack McMurdo steps off a train in Vermissa. The town lies in a coal valley where the hills are black and the sky is full of smoke.
McMurdo finds a room at the house of Jacob Shafter, a kind German who owns a shop. Shafter's daughter, Ettie, opens the door, and McMurdo cannot take his eyes off her.
That night McMurdo goes to the Union House, a saloon owned by Boss McGinty. McGinty is a huge, black-haired man, and everyone in the room seems to be afraid of him.
McMurdo speaks to McGinty without fear and says he left Chicago after serious trouble. McGinty enjoys his boldness and decides to take the stranger under his wing.
The Order of Freemen sounds like a friendly club that helps its members. In truth the Scowrers, its secret killers, use the Order to rule the whole valley by fear.
McMurdo is taken to the lodge hall at night and swears the oath of the Order. Afterwards the mark of the Freemen, a triangle in a circle, is burned into his arm.
At his first meeting McMurdo watches McGinty hand out dark jobs to the lodge, as if giving out work at a factory. He sees at once that the Order is a gang of killers.
Ted Baldwin, a young Scowrer, wanted to marry Ettie himself and hates the newcomer. When Baldwin attacks him, McMurdo draws a pistol, and McGinty laughs and takes McMurdo's side.
McMurdo and Ettie walk together beside the cold river and soon admit that they love each other. Ettie begs him to leave the Order and the valley before it destroys them both.
Across the valley, men are beaten, houses are burned and several people are murdered. Nobody speaks of it, because witnesses are afraid and juries are afraid, and the Scowrers go free.
A newspaper editor named James Stanger has written against the Scowrers in his paper. McGinty orders that he be taught a lesson, and McMurdo is told to join the group.
That night the masked men burst into the newspaper office and beat Stanger badly. He is hurt, but he is alive, and the people of the valley learn once more to be afraid.
A quiet lodge member named Morris takes McMurdo aside and confesses that he hates the killing. He wants to leave the valley, but he knows the Scowrers would never let him go.
At a meeting McGinty reads out a warning that the Pinkerton agency has sent a detective named Birdy Edwards to the valley. The Scowrers promise to find him and make sure he never leaves.
Ted Baldwin has never trusted McMurdo, and now he begins to speak openly against him. McMurdo calmly answers every charge, and the lodge decides that Baldwin is only jealous.
McMurdo tells Ettie that he will be leaving the Order very soon. He asks her to be ready for a sudden change and to trust him a little longer.
McMurdo tells McGinty that he knows where the Pinkerton man can be found. McGinty is delighted at the news, and he calls a great meeting of the whole lodge to deal with him.
On the chosen night the whole lodge fills the hall, and McGinty takes his seat at the head. Every man is eager to hear how the Pinkerton man will be caught.
McMurdo looks round the silent room and tells the Scowrers that they need not search for Birdy Edwards any longer. The man they have been hunting is standing right in front of them.
At that moment Captain Marvin and his police burst into the hall, with guns ready. The Scowrers are caught, and Boss McGinty is taken away in chains.
At the trial, Birdy Edwards tells the court everything he knows about the crimes of the Scowrers. Many of them are hanged or sent to prison, and the valley is free at last.
Ted Baldwin is not hanged, but he is sent to prison for years. He swears that when he is free he will find Edwards, even if it takes him the rest of his life.
Edwards marries Ettie and leaves the valley with her. They go to California, where he takes the name of John Douglas, and later move to England to find peace.
Douglas ends his story and says that Baldwin found him at last, in the peaceful house at Birlstone. Holmes thanks him and says that now everything is clear.
Holmes and the inspectors talk together about what the law will say. They agree that Douglas killed Baldwin in self-defence, and that no honest court would punish him.
Douglas decides that he will be safer far from England, and he books a place on a ship called the Palmyra. Holmes wishes him good luck and says a warm goodbye at the station.
Some time later the newspapers report that the Palmyra was struck by a storm at sea. John Douglas was lost overboard, and Holmes reads the news in silence.
Holmes tells Watson that he believes the brain of Moriarty stood behind the whole affair, although he cannot prove it. He promises himself that one day he will bring the professor down.
C1C2: The morning post brought Sherlock Holmes a puzzling letter, a column of numbers with a few plain words hidden among them, written in a hand he knew well. It came from Fred Porlock, a nervous informer who sold secrets to Holmes while serving a far more powerful master. Holmes turned the paper in the light with the delight of a man who has been handed a lock and told that the key lies somewhere in the room.

Holmes reasoned that a cipher built on numbers needs a book, and that Porlock would have chosen one which both of them could easily reach. He tried the great yearly reference work called Whitaker's Almanack, a thick volume of facts and figures that sits on the shelf of every thoughtful man. The first words that came out of its pages were the beginning of a message, and Holmes read them aloud with growing excitement.

When the words were set out on paper, they formed a short, urgent warning that danger was close at hand for a Mr Douglas, a wealthy country gentleman who lived at Birlstone House. The message broke off suddenly, as though Porlock had heard a step at his door and dared not write another word. Holmes tapped the page thoughtfully, for he knew that a warning of this kind seldom came without a reason.

Holmes spoke of Professor Moriarty, the Napoleon of crime, who sat like a spider at the centre of a vast web and felt every thread that trembled. The professor never stained his own hands with wrong, for his agents planned, stole and silenced men for him in every corner of London. It was to this unseen master that Porlock belonged, and Holmes could only guess what had made the little man risk a warning.

Holmes had scarcely finished speaking when Inspector MacDonald, a young Scottish detective whom he much admired, was shown into the room with troubled eyes. The news he carried was grave, for John Douglas, the master of Birlstone Manor in Sussex, had been found dead at midnight in his own study. Holmes laid down the deciphered message and quietly remarked that the warning had come a few hours too late.

On the journey into Sussex, MacDonald told them what he knew of Birlstone Manor, an ancient house of grey stone beside the quiet village of Birlstone. It was surrounded by a wide moat, crossed by a drawbridge which was drawn up each evening, so that no stranger could pass after dark. A man who wished to murder Douglas, the inspector admitted, had chosen a strange and difficult house to enter.

At Birlstone they were met by White Mason, the local inspector, a heavy and unhurried man who had been at work among the clues since dawn. He had refused to move anything until the London men arrived, and he told them so with the pride of a good craftsman. Holmes shook his hand warmly, for he knew how much a careless boot can destroy before a detective even enters a room.

A little before midnight, the quiet of the manor was broken by a heavy shot, and Cecil Barker, Douglas's closest friend, rushed downstairs with the butler Ames. In the study lay John Douglas, dead in his dressing gown, killed at close range by a shotgun that had been cut short for hiding under a coat. The only open window in the room looked out over the black water of the moat, and the drawbridge stood raised.

Beside the body lay a plain card bearing nothing but the letters V V and the number 341, written in a rough, hurried hand. On the dead man's forearm, partly hidden by his sleeve, was an old brand, a triangle set inside a circle, whose meaning White Mason could not even guess. Holmes looked at both marks for a long time, and then he asked, in his quiet voice, who had last seen them.

The weapon, a shotgun whose barrels had been sawn short so that it could be hidden beneath a coat, had been left behind on the floor. The window beside the body stood wide open, and on the sill there was the stain of a boot dipped in blood, as if the killer had stepped out into the night. It was all so plain and so convenient that Holmes began to distrust it at once.

Cecil Barker, a tall, handsome man who had been a close friend of the dead man since their days in California, said that Douglas had never lost his fear of old enemies from America. He believed that the murderer had entered through the open window and slipped away across the moat, since no one could have passed the raised drawbridge. He told the story with feeling, though Holmes noticed that he told it a little too smoothly.

Mrs Douglas, a graceful woman with a steady voice, bore the loss of her husband with a composure that astonished White Mason, who had seen many widows in his time. Barker, too, was strangely untroubled for a man who had lost his dearest friend only a few hours before. Holmes said nothing to either of them, but he filed both observations away in his memory as carefully as a clerk files a letter.

Leaving the study, Holmes walked slowly round the moat, bending over the bank below the open window with the patience of a hunter reading a trail. He found no trampled grass, no scrape of mud and no wet footmark anywhere on the far side, though a man who had fled through the water must have left some trace. The killer, it appeared, had gone neither across the moat nor away from the house.

In a corner of the study stood a heavy iron dumb-bell, one of the pair with which Douglas had kept himself strong, and Holmes lifted it with unusual interest. The second dumb-bell was nowhere to be found, and no one in the house could say when it had last been seen. Why should a murderer, in the middle of such a crime, trouble himself to carry away an old iron weight?

Holmes begged to be left alone, and for the rest of the night he sat in the silent study, smoking and turning the few facts over like coins in his hand. Each clue, he found, pointed in the direction in which the killer wished the police to look, and that was the very thing that troubled him. By morning he was convinced that the tidy story told at Birlstone had been built, piece by piece, by someone who knew exactly what the police would want to believe.

Early the next morning, at Holmes's request, White Mason's men dragged the bed of the moat beneath the study window with long poles. Presently they lifted from the water a sodden bundle of clothing, tied firmly round the very dumb-bell that had gone missing. Someone, it was clear, had needed a weight to carry those clothes to the bottom and keep them there.

Holmes told the two detectives that the bundle had held the dead man's own clothes, thrown into the moat so that no one could learn who he truly was. The man in the study, he explained, had been dressed in Douglas's gown and his face made unrecognisable, so that all would take him for the master of the house. Only one question remained, and Holmes put it quietly: where was the real John Douglas now?

Holmes found the household together and told them, in his gentlest voice, that the comedy was over and that he understood it entirely. The dead man was not John Douglas at all, he said, and Douglas himself had never left Birlstone Manor, but was hiding somewhere under its old roof. Mrs Douglas turned white, and Barker's face showed the relief of a man who is tired of a long and heavy secret.

At a word from Holmes, a hidden door in the old house swung open, and from the dark recess behind it stepped a broad, sunburned man in rough clothes. It was John Douglas, very much alive, and Mrs Douglas ran into his arms with a cry that made the hardened inspectors look away. He apologised to no one, but he looked at Holmes with a mixture of relief, respect and open admiration.

Douglas explained that the dead man was Ted Baldwin, an old enemy who had followed him across the sea and who entered the study that night armed with the sawn-off shotgun. In the desperate struggle over the weapon it had gone off, and it was Baldwin, not Douglas, who fell. The master of Birlstone swore that he had acted only to save his own life, and nobody in the room doubted him.

Douglas knew that Baldwin had friends as merciless as himself, and that he would never be safe once they learned that Baldwin had failed. With Barker and his wife he therefore made the dead man seem to be Douglas, dressing him in his own gown, leaving the card of the secret society on the floor, and sinking the stranger's clothes in the moat. Then he vanished into his hiding place, intending to let the world believe that he was dead.

Holmes asked the question that remained, which was why Baldwin had hunted Douglas across two continents for so many years. Douglas lit a pipe, drew breath, and said that the answer lay in a dark mining valley in Pennsylvania, where he had once lived under another name. What followed was a tale so strange that even Holmes forgot, for an hour, to look at the clock.

In the bitter winter of 1875, a bold young man who gave his name as Jack McMurdo stepped from the train into the town of Vermissa, in the heart of the Vermissa Valley. The valley was a land of coal and iron, with black hills scarred by mines, a sky stained by smoke, and a silence among its people that no stranger understood at first. McMurdo, with his cheerful face and his single bag, looked about him like a man who has come to a new place for a reason of his own.

McMurdo took a room in the house of Jacob Shafter, a gentle German storekeeper who asked few questions and who seemed to live in a quiet fear of something he did not name. His daughter Ettie opened the door, a lively, dark-haired girl with a clear and honest gaze, and from that moment the new lodger had hardly a thought for anything else. It was not a good moment to fall in love, but McMurdo was never a man to wait for the right time.

That evening McMurdo walked into the Union House, the most popular saloon in Vermissa, whose owner, Boss McGinty, was the most feared man in the valley. McGinty was a huge, black-haired fellow with a broad, hearty laugh, and every man in the crowded room watched his face before he allowed himself to smile. McMurdo noticed this, as he noticed everything, and he did not allow it to trouble his own easy manner.

McMurdo answered McGinty's questions without fear, hinting that he had left Chicago in a hurry after some serious trouble with the law. The great Bodymaster, who admired a man with a past and no apologies, laughed aloud and clapped him on the back as if they were old comrades. Before the night was over, McGinty had invited the newcomer to join a society in which, he said, good friends could always count on one another.

To the world, the Order of Freemen was a harmless brotherhood that gave help to its members in sickness and trouble, and it met each week in a public hall. Behind this respectable face, however, there lay a secret band known as the Scowrers, who struck down any man that dared to stand against them. Boss McGinty ruled them all, and the Scowrers, in turn, ruled the whole valley.

On a cold night, McMurdo was led into the lodge hall, where he swore terrible oaths of loyalty and silence in front of the whole gathering of Lodge 341. When the ceremony ended, the mark of the Order, a triangle within a circle, was burned into his forearm, so that every brother could know him. He bore the pain without a sound, and his steadiness won him the quiet respect of the room.

At his first lodge meeting, McMurdo sat quietly and listened while McGinty handed out his dark commissions like a foreman allotting work at a mine. Names were mentioned, places and nights were fixed, and men who were absent were doomed with the same calm voice that read the minutes of the last meeting. McMurdo kept his face still, though he now understood the exact nature of the society he had joined.

Ted Baldwin, a swaggering young Scowrer, had long hoped to marry Ettie Shafter, and he hated the stranger who had taken the room beneath her father's roof. When the quarrel boiled over in McGinty's saloon, McMurdo leaped up, seized the other man by the throat, and held a pistol under his chin. McGinty, to everyone's surprise, burst into laughter and declared that the new brother was worth any two of the old ones.

Day by day, McMurdo and Ettie grew closer, and on a walk beside the frozen river they at last admitted what each of them already knew. Ettie, who hated everything the Scowrers stood for, begged him to leave the Order and the valley while there was still time. He answered that he could not yet go, and he asked her, with an earnestness that she did not understand, to trust him.

Across the valley the same story was repeated, as shopkeepers, mine bosses and policemen were beaten, burned out of their homes or even murdered in the night. No witness dared to give evidence, no jury dared to convict, and the Scowrers walked the streets as freely as honest men. It was a land governed by terror, and the people who lived in it had learned to bow their heads and keep silent.

James Stanger, the editor of the local newspaper, had dared to print the truth about the Scowrers and their crimes, and for this he was marked by the lodge. McGinty decided that the man must be taught a lesson, and the task was given to a group of brothers that included the newest member. McMurdo accepted it without a word, because a man who refuses is a man who is suspected.

That night, a group of masked men burst into the newspaper office and beat James Stanger until he could no longer rise from the floor. The editor survived, though he was badly hurt, and the message of the attack passed quickly through every house and shop in the valley. It was the lesson that McGinty had wanted, and McMurdo had taken part in it only to keep his place among the brothers.

Morris, a thoughtful and educated member of the lodge, drew McMurdo aside one evening and confessed that the violence was destroying his peace of mind. He longed to leave the valley with his family, but he knew too well that the Scowrers did not permit anyone to walk away. McMurdo listened with sympathy and said little, for he was weighing carefully how far he could trust the man.

At the next meeting of the lodge, McGinty rose with a grave face and told his brothers that the great Pinkerton detective agency had sent a spy among them. The man's name, he said, was Birdy Edwards, a clever and fearless detective who had broken more than one band of criminals before. The Scowrers vowed to find him, and none of them doubted what would happen when they did.

Ted Baldwin had never trusted his rival, and with the arrival of the Pinkerton rumour his suspicions found a voice. He accused McMurdo before the lodge of being too clever, too calm and too fond of asking questions, but he had no proof to offer. McMurdo answered every charge with a smile, and the brothers agreed that Baldwin was speaking out of jealousy alone.

McMurdo told Ettie that the days of the Scowrers were numbered and that he would soon be free of them. He asked her to be ready for a sudden change in their lives, and to keep faith in him though everything around her might make it seem unwise. She searched his face for a long moment and, with a deep breath, gave him her word, whatever might come.

McMurdo went to the Bodymaster and calmly announced that he knew how Birdy Edwards might be found and captured. McGinty, delighted at the news and flattered by his new favourite's cleverness, called a meeting of the whole lodge to arrange the matter. Nothing in the visitor's manner suggested that he was walking into a danger greater than any he had ever faced.

On the appointed night the whole of the lodge crowded into the hall, where the lamps burned low and the air was heavy with tobacco and expectation. McGinty took his place at the head of the room, and every brother leaned forward to learn how the hated detective would be caught. McMurdo rose to speak, and for a moment he stood quite still, as if gathering himself for a leap.

McMurdo looked slowly round the crowded room, and when the last whisper had died, he calmly told the Scowrers that they need not search for Birdy Edwards any longer. He was Birdy Edwards, a detective of the Pinkerton agency, and the mask that he had worn for so many months was now laid aside. There was a silence that seemed to last a year, and then every man in the room sprang to his feet.

At that moment the doors of the hall were flung open, and Captain Marvin of the Coal and Iron Police marched in with a body of armed men. The Scowrers, caught like rats in their own trap, found no way of escape, and the great Boss McGinty was led away in chains with his proud face grey. Nothing in all his years of power had prepared him for this one night.

At the trial, Birdy Edwards stood before the court and told everything that he had seen and learned during his months among the Scowrers. His evidence was clear, and the juries, no longer afraid, delivered their judgments, so that several of the leaders were hanged and many others sent to prison. The power that had held the Vermissa Valley in its fist for years was broken at last.

Ted Baldwin escaped the gallows, but he was sentenced to many years behind bars, and in his cell he nursed a single hatred. He swore that on the day he walked free he would find the man who had betrayed the lodge, and that no ocean or mountain should stop him. It was an oath that Birdy Edwards could not have known would stay alive for so very long.

Edwards married Ettie, and the two left the valley, changing their names and their homes more than once to escape the hatred that followed them. In California he became John Douglas, a prosperous mining man, and in time he crossed the sea to England and settled in the quiet house at Birlstone. He hoped that an ocean might do what the law could not, but Baldwin was already on his track.

Douglas ended his tale with a sigh, and the listeners found that the lamp had burned low and that the evening had slipped away. He told them that Baldwin had followed him at last into the peace of Birlstone, and that the rest they already knew. Holmes thanked him with real feeling, for the long and dark road of the story had at last led back to the study and the moat.

Holmes and the inspectors talked quietly together about what the law would make of Douglas's action, and they agreed that it was plainly a case of self-defence. No honest jury, they thought, would punish a man for killing in order not to be killed, though the false report would need an explanation. Douglas, for his part, was less concerned with the law than with the friends of Baldwin, who might still be waiting.

Douglas decided that he would never be wholly safe while enemies remained alive, and he resolved to travel to a distant land and start his life again. He booked a passage on the steamship Palmyra, which was bound for South Africa, and Holmes shook his hand with real warmth on the eve of departure. The detective felt, though he did not say so, that the story had not yet finished.

Some weeks later the papers reported that the steamship Palmyra had met with a violent storm and that John Douglas had been lost overboard in the darkness. Holmes read the account in silence, laid the paper on his knee, and sat for some time looking at the fire. The man had escaped the Scowrers, the hatred of Baldwin and the justice of the law, only to be taken by the sea.

Holmes turned to Watson and said that he believed the cold hand of Moriarty had lain behind the whole affair, though no proof of it would ever be found. The professor sat at the centre of his web, and the strange events at Birlstone were only one trembling thread among many. Holmes stood by the window, looking out at the fog on Baker Street, and vowed that the day would come when he would put an end to the Napoleon of crime.
